8700:
To ingest something means to take it into the body — most often through the mouth, by swallowing. It is the formal, precise word for what happens when you eat food, drink water, take a pill, or accidentally swallow something you didn't mean to.

A simple way to picture it: imagine the body as a container with an opening at the top (the mouth). To ingest something is to move it from the outside world into that container, where the body will then deal with it.

The one doing the ingesting is always a living organism. A person ingests medicine. An animal ingests its prey. Even a single cell in biology can ingest bacteria — the cell literally surrounds and absorbs the bacteria — and scientists use the word "ingest" to describe this too.

Almost any substance that enters the body through the mouth can be described as ingested: food, water, medicine, alcohol, poison, a foreign object (like when a child accidentally swallows a small toy), and even gases or fumes in certain scientific contexts. The word is not limited to food — this is exactly what makes it both powerful and precise.

These words are close relatives, but they are not the same.

"Eat" is casual and specific to food. You eat a sandwich. You wouldn't normally say you "eat" a pill or "eat" poison.

"Drink" is specific to liquids.

"Swallow" describes the physical, mechanical action of moving something down your throat. It focuses on how something goes in, not what happens after.

"Ingest" is broader than all of these. It covers any substance — food, liquid, medication, poison, or an object — taken into the body. And unlike "swallow," it doesn't focus on the physical motion but on the outcome: the substance is now inside the body's system. This is precisely why doctors, scientists, and toxicologists prefer "ingest" — it is accurate regardless of what the substance is.

"Ingest" is a formal and clinical word. You won't hear it much in everyday conversation — nobody says "I just ingested a burger." You will find it in medical writing ("Do not ingest more than the recommended dose"), on product warning labels ("Harmful if ingested"), in toxicology reports ("If ingested, seek immediate medical attention"), and in biology textbooks ("The organism ingests nutrients from the surrounding environment").
The Technical Meaning in Computers and Data

In technology and data science, "ingest" has taken on a second, extended meaning. When a computer system ingests data, it means the system is taking in large amounts of data from an external source in order to store, process, or analyze it. For example: "The pipeline ingests thousands of records per second," or "The AI model ingests training data before it can learn." This is a direct metaphor borrowed from the biological meaning — just as a body takes in food and processes it into energy and nutrients, a computer system takes in raw data and processes it into something useful.

The noun form of "ingest" is ingestion, referring to the act or process of ingesting. "Ingestion of alcohol on an empty stomach can be dangerous." "The ingestion of the medication should be followed by a full glass of water." This form appears constantly in medical, scientific, and legal writing, so it is just as worth knowing as the verb itself.

To ingest means to take a substance into the body — typically by swallowing — so the body can process it. In technology, it means to take data into a system for processing. It is a formal, precise word that works for food, medicine, poison, foreign objects, and even data, making it far more versatile than everyday words like "eat" or "drink."
8701:
An inglenook is a cozy, sheltered seating area built into the wall beside or around a large, open fireplace. Think of it as a little private nook — a semi-enclosed alcove — that wraps around a hearth, with benches or seats on either side, so you can sit right next to the fire and feel completely enveloped in warmth.

The key idea is that it is not just the fireplace itself. It is the entire snug little space that surrounds the fireplace — the recessed area, the seating, and the sense of being tucked away from the rest of the room.

Imagine a large stone fireplace in an old farmhouse. Instead of the fireplace sitting flush with the wall, the wall is built outward around it, creating a deep, cave-like recess. Inside this recess, on the left and right sides of the fire, there are low wooden benches or stone seats built into the walls. You can walk into this space, sit down on those benches, stretch your legs toward the flame, and feel the heat all around you. The rest of the room is behind you. You are surrounded on three sides — by wall, by stone, by fire. That sheltered, fire-hugging space is the inglenook.

For something to qualify as an inglenook, it generally has these characteristics:

  • A recess or alcove. The space is set back into the wall, not open to the whole room. It feels enclosed, like a little room within a room.
  • A large fireplace at its center. Inglenooks are always built around an open hearth — and these hearths are typically big and deep, not the small, decorative fireplaces common in modern homes.
  • Built-in seating on the sides. The benches or seats are part of the architecture itself, running along the side walls of the nook. They are not chairs you bring in — they are baked into the structure.
  • A low ceiling overhead (often). The roof of the nook — formed by the chimney breast above — often hangs lower than the rest of the room, adding to the sense of being enclosed and sheltered.

Inglenooks belong to older architecture, particularly in Britain and parts of rural Europe. You find them most commonly in:

  • Old English cottages and farmhouses, especially from the medieval and Tudor periods
  • Traditional country pubs in Britain — where they are beloved spots to sit with a drink by the fire
  • Manor houses and castles with grand stone fireplaces
  • Historical buildings and heritage properties

In modern times, inglenooks are sometimes recreated in new homes as a design feature — because people still find them deeply appealing — but they are a distinctly old-fashioned, rustic architectural element.

The word inglenook does a lot of emotional work. It is not a neutral, clinical term. When you use or hear this word, it brings with it a whole atmosphere:

  • Warmth — not just physical, but emotional
  • Intimacy — it is a space for small groups, quiet conversations, or solitude
  • Safety and shelter — being tucked away from the cold, the dark, and the outside world
  • Nostalgia and charm — it evokes old, simpler times

This is why writers love the word. It does not just describe a place; it conjures a feeling.
How It's Used in a Sentence

Here are natural examples of inglenook in use:

  • "The old inn had a beautiful inglenook where guests would gather after a long day of walking through the moors."
  • "She curled up in the inglenook with a book while the storm raged outside."
  • "The cottage's most charming feature was the inglenook beside the kitchen hearth, still fitted with the original oak settle."
  • "The estate agent described the living room as having an original Tudor inglenook fireplace."

This is a distinction worth being clear about:

ConceptWhat it is
FireplaceThe opening in a wall where fire burns — just the hearth itself
InglenookThe entire recessed space around and beside the fireplace, including the seating area

Every inglenook contains a fireplace, but not every fireplace has an inglenook. A small, flat fireplace set into a modern wall with no alcove, no seating, and no recess is just a fireplace. An inglenook is a fully developed, architecturally built-out environment centered on that fire.

An inglenook is a snug, recessed alcove built around a large fireplace — with benches tucked into the sides — designed so that people can sit close to the fire and feel warmly enclosed. It is a feature of old, traditional buildings and carries a powerful sense of coziness, shelter, and charm.
8702: Something is inglorious when it brings shame or dishonor instead of pride and respect — or when it passes through life completely unnoticed and unrecognized, without leaving any mark of greatness behind.

"Inglorious" carries two related but distinct meanings, and understanding both is key.

The first and more common meaning is: shameful, disgraceful, or dishonoring.

This is when something is done — or ends — in a way that brings shame rather than pride. It's not just bad. It's specifically bad in a way that damages honor, dignity, or reputation. There's a moral weight to it.

Think of a soldier who runs away from a battle in fear, abandoning his comrades. That's not just an unsuccessful act — it's an inglorious one, because it involves cowardice and dishonor. Or imagine a celebrated politician whose career ends because he's caught taking bribes. That's an inglorious end — not just a sad one, but a shameful, undignified one.

The key idea here is that inglorious doesn't just mean "things went badly." It means things went badly in a way that reflects poorly on the character or conduct of the person involved.

The second meaning is: obscure, unknown, forgotten — without fame or recognition.

This is a quieter, more sorrowful use of the word. A person can live an inglorious life not because they did anything shameful, but simply because the world never noticed them. They lived, they worked, they died — and no one remembered. No glory ever came their way.

This meaning is less about shame and more about invisibility. The great English poet Thomas Gray captured this idea beautifully when he wrote about ordinary village people who were buried and forgotten — talented souls who never got the chance to shine. Their lives were inglorious not because they were bad people, but because history simply passed them by.
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

"Inglorious" is often confused with words like shameful, disgraceful, humiliating, or undistinguished. Here's how it stands apart:

Shameful and disgraceful are blunter. They simply say something is wrong or embarrassing. Inglorious is more specific — it's about the absence or loss of glory. It measures things against a standard of honor, valor, or greatness, and notes the failure to reach it.

Undistinguished means plain or unremarkable — just average. But inglorious carries much more emotional weight. An undistinguished career is just a boring one. An inglorious career is one that ended in scandal, failure, or complete obscurity.

Humiliating refers to the feeling of shame in the moment. Inglorious is more lasting — it's a judgment on the overall nature of something, not just how it felt at the time.
The Emotional and Moral Weight of the Word

"Inglorious" is not a casual, everyday word. It's formal and literary, with a solemn, almost grave tone. When you call something inglorious, you are passing a serious judgment — you're saying it failed to live up to what honor, dignity, or greatness required.

It often implies a sense of what could have been. An inglorious defeat isn't just a loss — it's a loss that was made worse by cowardice, poor choices, or disgraceful conduct. An inglorious end to a great career isn't just sad — it's a tragic fall from the heights of what someone once was. There is often a feeling of wasted potential or betrayed promise in the word.

Here are clear examples to show you exactly how the word works in real sentences:

"The army's inglorious retreat — soldiers throwing down their weapons and fleeing in panic — was a humiliation the nation would never forget." (Shameful, disgraceful meaning.)

"His once-promising career came to an inglorious end when he was exposed as a fraud." (A dishonorable downfall.)

"She lived an inglorious life in a small town, her extraordinary mind never discovered by the world." (Unknown and unrecognized, without any positive/negative moral judgment.)

"It was one of the most inglorious chapters in the company's history — years of corruption, cover-ups, and betrayal." (A period defined by dishonor.)

"He lost the championship in the most inglorious fashion — not through bad luck, but through sheer laziness and arrogance." (The manner of failure made it shameful.)

The word "inglorious" always measures something against a standard of glory, honor, or greatness. You can only call something inglorious if there was an expectation — or at least a possibility — of something better. That's what gives the word its sting. It's not just failure. It's failure with a sense of what was owed, what was possible, and what was lost.
8703:
An ingot is a solid block of metal that has been melted down and poured into a mold to harden into a simple, convenient shape — usually a rectangle or a bar — so it can be stored, transported, or processed further.

Think of it this way: imagine you collected a huge pile of scrap metal — old car parts, broken tools, metal scraps of all shapes and sizes. That pile is messy, uneven, and nearly impossible to measure, store neatly, or work with. Now imagine you melt all of it down into a liquid and pour it into a rectangular brick mold, like an ice cube tray, and let it cool. What you get when it hardens is an ingot — a clean, solid, uniform block of metal that is easy to handle.

An ingot is most commonly shaped like a rectangular brick or a thick bar. It is deliberately kept in this plain, simple shape because the goal is not to make something decorative or functional yet — the goal is just to make the metal manageable. Think of the classic gold bars you see in movies stacked inside a bank vault. Those are gold ingots. They are smooth, dense, heavy, and shaped like thick bricks.

The size and weight of an ingot can vary enormously depending on its purpose. A gold ingot held in bank vaults (called a "good delivery" bar) weighs about 400 troy ounces — roughly 12.4 kilograms, or 27 pounds. But smaller ingots can weigh just a few grams. On the industrial end, steel ingots used in factories can weigh several tonnes.

The process is straightforward:

  1. Metal is heated in a furnace until it melts into a liquid.
  2. The liquid metal is poured into a mold — a container shaped like a brick, bar, or block.
  3. It is left to cool and solidify, hardening into that shape.
  4. The solid block is removed from the mold. That block is the ingot.

This is sometimes called casting. The mold determines the shape, and the shape is always kept simple on purpose.
What Metals Are Made Into Ingots?

Almost any metal can be formed into an ingot. The most commonly known ones are:

  • Gold — the classic image of wealth stored as ingots in vaults
  • Silver — similarly stored and traded as ingots
  • Steel — massively produced in industry for making cars, buildings, and machines
  • Aluminum — widely used ingots that get turned into countless products
  • Copper — used in electrical and industrial applications
  • Platinum and other precious metals
Why Do Ingots Exist? What's the Point?

Ingots exist because they solve a practical problem: how do you store, move, and measure metal efficiently?

Raw ore dug from the ground is full of impurities and comes in irregular lumps. Scrap metal is all different shapes and sizes. Neither is easy to work with. An ingot solves this by giving metal a clean, standardized form. Here's why that matters:

  • Storage: Rectangular blocks stack neatly and take up predictable space.
  • Transport: A uniform shape is far easier to move and load than irregular chunks.
  • Measurement: Because an ingot is one solid piece, its weight and purity can be measured and certified. This is critical in trade — a gold ingot can be stamped with its weight and purity so buyers know exactly what they are getting.
  • Further manufacturing: Factories need metal in a clean, ready-to-use form. An ingot is that form. It can be melted again and reshaped into specific products.
The Ingot's Role in the Bigger Picture

An ingot is essentially a middle step in the life of metal. It sits between raw ore (the beginning) and a finished product (the end).

Raw ore → Ingot → Finished product

For example, aluminum ore is mined, refined, and cast into aluminum ingots. Those ingots are then sent to factories where they are melted again, rolled into sheets, and eventually turned into airplane parts, drink cans, window frames, or kitchen foil.

The ingot itself is not a final product. Nobody uses an ingot directly in their daily life. It is an intermediate, standardized form of metal waiting to be turned into something else.

Ingots — especially gold and silver ones — have historically been used as a form of stored wealth and traded commodity. Because an ingot has a measurable, certifiable weight and purity, it can be bought and sold like a financial asset. Central banks around the world hold gold ingots in their reserves. Investors buy silver ingots as a store of value. In this context, an ingot is almost like a very heavy, very dense coin — a universally understood unit of valuable metal.

An ingot is a block of metal made by melting metal down and letting it harden in a mold into a simple shape, created purely for the practical purpose of making metal easy to store, transport, trade, and process further.
8704:
To ingrain something means to fix a habit, belief, attitude, or way of thinking so deeply into a person's mind or character that it becomes a permanent part of who they are — almost impossible to remove or change.

Think of it like pressing ink into fabric. If ink only sits on the surface, you can wipe it off easily. But if it seeps all the way into the fibers of the cloth, it becomes part of the fabric itself — washing it won't help much. That's exactly what ingraining does to the mind. It takes something and presses it so deep that it stops being something a person has and becomes something a person is.

Here's an important practical note: in everyday English, "ingrain" is almost always used in its past participle form — "ingrained" — and it usually appears with the word deeply.

You'll rarely hear someone say "This experience will ingrain fear in him" (though it's grammatically correct). Far more often, you'll hear: "He has a deeply ingrained fear."

So while ingrain is the verb, ingrained (used as an adjective or in passive constructions) is the form you'll encounter most in real life.

Ingraining always involves something mental or behavioral — not physical objects. Things that get ingrained include:

Habits, beliefs, values, biases, fears, attitudes, customs, and ways of thinking. Essentially, anything that lives in the mind or shapes how a person behaves.
The Three Key Ideas Inside This Word

Understanding "ingrain" fully means understanding three things that are always implied whenever the word is used:

1. Depth. Something ingrained isn't shallow or surface-level. It has gone deep — into the core of a person's character or thinking. A passing thought is not ingrained. A belief you've held since childhood, without even questioning it, probably is.

2. Resistance to change. Because it's so deep, something ingrained is very hard to undo. People often struggle for years — sometimes with professional help — to overcome ingrained fears, biases, or unhealthy habits. The word quietly signals: this won't be easy to remove.

3. Formation over time (usually). Most ingrained things are built through repetition — doing the same thing again and again, hearing the same message year after year, living in the same environment for a long time. However, a single powerful or traumatic experience can also ingrain something instantly.
Ingrained Can Be Positive or Negative

This word doesn't judge. It simply describes depth and permanence. So ingrained things can be wonderful or harmful:

Positive: A child raised in a household that always showed kindness might grow up with an ingrained sense of empathy. That's a beautiful thing.

Negative: Someone raised in an environment full of prejudice might grow up with ingrained biases they don't even realize they carry. That's damaging — and hard to fix precisely because it feels "normal" to them.

"Decades of living alone had ingrained certain habits in her that she couldn't shake even after she got married."

"The coach's early training ingrained discipline in the players."

"He had a deeply ingrained belief that asking for help was a sign of weakness."

"Racism was so deeply ingrained in the institution that even well-meaning employees unconsciously perpetuated it."

"Her fear of public speaking was ingrained from a humiliating experience in third grade."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Instill means to gradually put a quality or idea into someone's mind — usually done gently and deliberately, often by a parent or teacher. "She instilled confidence in her students." Instill focuses on the act of putting something in. Ingrain focuses more on how deep and permanent the result is. Something instilled can become ingrained over time.

Embed means to fix something firmly inside something else. It's used more broadly (you can embed a chip in a device, for instance). Ingrain is specifically about the mind, character, or culture — and carries a stronger sense of being hard to reverse.

To ingrain something is to press a habit, belief, or attitude so deep into a person's mind or character — usually through repetition over time — that it becomes a fixed, almost unremovable part of them.
8705:
When something is ingrained, it means it has become so deeply fixed into a person's mind, character, or way of life — or into a culture or society — that it is very hard to change or get rid of.

Think of it this way: imagine pressing ink so hard into a piece of cloth that it doesn't just sit on the surface — it sinks deep into every fiber. Even if you wash it, it won't come out easily. That's exactly what "ingrained" captures. Something ingrained isn't sitting on the surface. It has gone deep inside, become a firm part of something, and resists being removed.

The word is used for things that live inside a person's mind or character, or inside a group/society. The most common things described as ingrained are:

  • Habits — "He had an ingrained habit of checking his phone first thing every morning, even on vacation."
  • Beliefs — "Her ingrained belief that hard work always pays off guided every decision she made."
  • Attitudes — "His ingrained attitude of distrust toward strangers made it difficult for him to make new friends."
  • Prejudices or biases — "The ingrained prejudice against outsiders had existed in that community for generations."
  • Values — "Honesty was so ingrained in her that she felt physically uncomfortable telling even a small lie."
  • Fear — "After years of being criticized, an ingrained fear of failure stopped him from even trying."
The Key Quality: Depth + Resistance to Change

Two things are always true when something is described as ingrained:

1. It went deep over time.
Ingrained things are almost never sudden. They develop slowly — through years of repetition, upbringing, culture, experience, or environment. A belief you formed last week is not ingrained. A belief you've held since childhood, reinforced thousands of times, absolutely can be.

2. It is hard to uproot.
Because something ingrained is so deeply embedded, simply wanting to change it is rarely enough. It takes serious, deliberate, sustained effort — and even then, it may linger.

This is the heart of the word: depth that resists removal.

It can be either, depending on context. The word itself is neutral — it just tells you how deeply fixed something is.

  • Negative: "His ingrained arrogance cost him every relationship he ever had."
  • Positive: "Her ingrained sense of fairness made her a beloved leader."
  • Neutral: "The ingrained customs of the village had been passed down for centuries."

So pay attention to the word it's describing — that will tell you whether it's a good or bad thing.

You will often see or hear "deeply ingrained" as a pair. This just adds extra emphasis to show how extremely fixed something is. It's a natural, very widely used intensifier.

"Racism, in many societies, is deeply ingrained and cannot be solved with a single law."

You can use "ingrained" alone and it already implies depth — but "deeply ingrained" makes it even stronger and more emphatic.

Less commonly, "ingrained" is also used literally for physical dirt or grime that has worked its way deep into a surface and is very difficult to clean.

"No matter how hard she scrubbed, the ingrained dirt in the old tile floor would not come out."

This physical image is actually the clearest way to feel the word — dirt that is not just sitting on top, but has been ground down deep into the material. This is exactly the same logic applied to the non-physical (mental, emotional, cultural) uses.
Synonyms That Help You Understand It Better

Knowing similar words can sharpen your understanding:

  • Deep-seated — fixed deep inside, especially feelings or beliefs
  • Deep-rooted — like a tree with roots so deep it cannot be pulled out
  • Entrenched — dug in so firmly it resists any attempt to move it
  • Hardwired — built in so fundamentally it feels like it's part of the structure itself

All of these share the same spirit: so fixed, for so long, that change is genuinely difficult.

If something is ingrained, it has been pressed so deeply into a person, culture, or material — usually over a long time — that it has become a firm, stubborn part of it, and is very difficult to change or remove.
8706:
An ingrate is a person who receives kindness, help, generosity, or favors from others but shows no gratitude in return. They take what is given to them and act as though it was owed to them, or as though nothing was ever done for them at all.

Think of it this way: someone sacrifices their time, money, or energy to help another person — and that other person never acknowledges it, never appreciates it, and moves on as if it never happened. That second person is an ingrate.

This is important: an ingrate is not simply someone who forgets to say thank you once. That would be a small, human lapse. An ingrate has a deeper character flaw — a consistent inability or unwillingness to recognize what others have done for them.

An ingrate often:

  • Takes help for granted, as if they deserved it
  • Never acknowledges the sacrifice or effort behind what they received
  • May even turn against the very people who helped them — speaking badly of them, cutting them off, or taking advantage of them again

This is why there is a famous phrase: "biting the hand that feeds you." An ingrate is exactly this kind of person.
The emotional weight of the word

"Ingrate" is not a neutral, descriptive word. It is a word of moral condemnation. When someone calls another person an ingrate, they are expressing hurt, disappointment, or strong disapproval. They are saying: "This person has a moral failing. They do not value what was given to them."

It is a heavier, sharper word than simply saying "ungrateful person." It sounds like an accusation — almost like a verdict on someone's character.

"Ingrate" is a slightly formal or literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in books, formal writing, or dramatic speech than in casual conversation. In everyday talk, people might say "ungrateful so-and-so" or just "he's so ungrateful." But when someone reaches for the word "ingrate," they are making a stronger, more pointed statement.
Who typically uses this word, and when

It is almost always used by someone who:

  • Has personally been treated with ingratitude, or
  • Is an observer who finds the lack of gratitude morally wrong

A parent exhausted by a child who never appreciates their sacrifice might say it. A mentor who poured years into a student who then dismissed them might use it. A friend who gave everything and received nothing might call the other person an ingrate.

• "She spent years supporting him financially and emotionally. When he finally got on his feet, he never looked back. What an ingrate."
  • "The ingrate didn't even attend the funeral of the man who had funded his entire education."
  • "After all the city had done for him, he publicly insulted its people. History would remember him as an ingrate."
  • "I don't want to raise an ingrate — I want my children to appreciate what they have."
The opposite of an ingrate is simply a grateful person — someone who recognizes what has been done for them, feels thankful for it, and expresses that thanks in some meaningful way.

An ingrate is a person who is given something valuable — whether it is help, love, money, time, or opportunity — and feels or shows no gratitude for it. The word implies not just a single thoughtless moment but a character trait: a fundamental failure to value what others have done. It is a word loaded with moral judgment, and using it signals that the speaker feels wronged or deeply disappointed by someone's lack of appreciation.
8707:
To ingratiate yourself means to deliberately make someone like you or approve of you — usually through flattery, excessive helpfulness, charm, or pleasing behavior — often because you want to gain something from them, like power, money, a promotion, or social acceptance.

The key idea is that the behavior is calculated and self-serving, not genuinely kind. The person doing it has a hidden motive: get this person on my side so I can benefit.
How It Is Almost Always Used

This verb almost always appears in one specific pattern:

ingratiate + [reflexive pronoun] + with + [person]

The reflexive pronoun (myself, yourself, himself, herself, themselves) is almost always required. You don't ingratiate someone else — you ingratiate yourself with someone. Think of it as directing the action back at yourself: you are the one making yourself more likable in someone else's eyes.

Examples:

  • She tried to ingratiate herself with her new boss by volunteering for every task.
  • He ingratiated himself with the wealthy family by constantly praising their home and lifestyle.
  • The new student ingratiated himself with the popular group by always agreeing with whatever they said.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is crucial: ingratiate almost always carries a negative or suspicious tone. When you use this word to describe someone's behavior, you are usually implying that:

  • Their niceness is fake or exaggerated
  • They are not being genuine — they are performing kindness
  • They have an ulterior motive — they want something
  • Their behavior is a little shameless or undignified

If someone is simply being kind, you would not use this word. You use "ingratiate" when the kindness feels strategic, excessive, or hollow.

A good employee who works hard to impress their boss → not ingratiation.
An employee who showers the boss with compliments, laughs at every joke, and brings them coffee every morning specifically to get a promotion → ingratiation.

The difference is sincerity. Ingratiation is niceness used as a tool.

Ingratiation is what people informally describe as:

  • "sucking up"
  • "buttering someone up"
  • "brown-nosing"
  • "currying favor"

These phrases all describe the same act: performing charm or helpfulness to win someone's approval for personal gain. "Ingratiate" is simply the formal, more sophisticated way to say the same thing.

• Ingratiating (adjective) — describes behavior or manner that is designed to win favor. "He had an ingratiating smile — the kind that made you feel like he wanted something." It can also be used neutrally or even positively to mean "charming," but the suspicious undertone is usually still present.
  • Ingratiatingly (adverb) — in a manner meant to win favor. "She spoke ingratiatingly, agreeing with everything the director said."
  • Ingratiation (noun) — the act itself. "His ingratiation with the committee was obvious to everyone."

Ingratiation is different from simply being likable. A naturally warm and friendly person is not ingratiating — they are just pleasant. Ingratiation implies conscious strategy. The person has made a decision: "I will behave in this specific way to make this specific person like me so I can get what I want."

This is why the word tends to sound slightly contemptuous. It strips the "niceness" of its moral value, because the niceness isn't really about the other person at all — it's about the self.
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

After the new manager arrived, David suddenly started arriving early, complimenting her decisions in every meeting, and offering to handle her administrative tasks. Everyone in the office could see he was simply trying to ingratiate himself with her before the annual performance reviews.

Notice what this sentence tells you: David's behavior changed because of a motive. It wasn't who he naturally was. He was performing — and doing it transparently enough that his coworkers saw right through it. That is the essence of the word.
8708:
When you describe something — a person's behavior, smile, tone, or manner — as ingratiating, you mean that it is clearly, and often too obviously, designed to make someone feel pleased, flattered, or charmed, so that the person doing it can gain favor, approval, or advantage in return.

Think of it this way: imagine someone who is trying really hard to be liked — not because they are naturally warm and friendly, but because they want something, or they want to be seen in a good light. The behavior that results from that effort is ingratiating.
The Most Important Thing to Understand: It Has a Sting in It

This is where most learners go wrong, so pay close attention.

"Ingratiating" is not a compliment. It is not simply another word for "charming," "friendly," or "polite." When you call someone's behavior ingratiating, you are quietly suggesting that it is calculated and self-serving — that the warmth or flattery is not fully genuine, but rather a strategy to win someone over.

The word carries a subtle sense of suspicion and disapproval. You're saying, in effect: "I can see what you're doing, and it feels a little fake."

So if someone calls your smile "charming," that is a compliment. If they call it "ingratiating," they are politely implying it looks put-on and deliberate.
A Simple, Clear Way to Picture It

Imagine a new employee at a company. On their very first day, they tell the boss how brilliant his ideas are, laugh loudly at every one of his jokes even when they aren't funny, offer to get him coffee constantly, and agree with everything he says — all with a wide, eager smile.

Their behavior is ingratiating. They are performing friendliness and admiration with the goal of being liked and getting ahead, not because they genuinely feel it.

Now, here's the important part: the people watching this will feel slightly uncomfortable, because it all feels a little too smooth, a little too deliberate. That awkward, slightly-too-sweet quality is exactly what "ingratiating" captures.
What Can Be Described as Ingratiating?

The adjective is flexible and can describe many things:

  • A manner: "He spoke in an ingratiating manner, agreeing with everything she said."
  • A smile: "She walked in with an ingratiating smile, clearly hoping to be forgiven."
  • A tone of voice: "His ingratiating tone made it obvious he wanted a favor."
  • A person: "He was a slippery, ingratiating man whom no one quite trusted."
  • Behavior in general: "Her ingratiating behavior at the party impressed no one — it was all too obvious."
The Spectrum: From Mildly Charming to Deeply Sycophantic

It helps to see "ingratiating" as sitting on a scale:

At one end, you have someone who is simply friendly and warm — that is genuine, and no one calls it ingratiating.

Move a little further, and the friendliness starts to feel slightly calculated — a little too eager, a little too flattering. This is the territory of ingratiating.

At the far end of the scale, you have someone who is utterly shameless in their flattery, a complete yes-man — that is sycophantic (an even stronger, harsher word).

So "ingratiating" sits comfortably in the middle: not innocent warmth, but not quite as extreme as total shamelessness. It is charm that has a visible agenda behind it.
Can It Ever Be Neutral or Positive?

Very rarely, and only in specific contexts. For example, if you say:

"The puppy's ingratiating behavior — rolling over and licking everyone's hands — made it impossible not to adopt him."

Here, the word is used with a kind of gentle amusement. The puppy is shamelessly charming, and it works. In this use, the tone is affectionate rather than critical.

However, this softer use is the exception. When describing people, particularly adults, "ingratiating" almost always carries a negative or at least suspicious tone.
How It Is Different From Similar Words

• Charming — genuinely attractive and pleasant. A compliment. No hidden agenda implied.
  • Flattering — saying nice things about someone. Can be sincere or slightly calculated, but not as loaded as ingratiating.
  • Obsequious — extremely eager to serve or please; almost like a servant desperate for approval. Stronger and more negative than ingratiating.
  • Sycophantic — shameless, excessive flattery purely for self-gain. The harshest of the group.
  • Ingratiating — deliberately and noticeably trying to win favor, with an air of calculation and insincerity. Sits between "flattering" and "obsequious."
A Few More Example Sentences to Seal It In

• "The salesman's ingratiating charm made the customers uneasy rather than comfortable."
  • "She gave an ingratiating laugh at the director's weak joke, hoping to be cast in the film."
  • "Despite his ingratiating manner, no one in the office actually trusted him."
  • "The politician's ingratiating speech, full of compliments for the audience, felt hollow and rehearsed."

Ingratiating means behaving in a way that is deliberately and often obviously designed to make someone like you or approve of you — usually for your own benefit — so that the behavior ends up feeling calculated, insincere, or a little too smooth.

Ingratiation is the act of deliberately trying to make yourself liked or favored by someone — usually someone who has power, influence, or something you want. In the simplest terms, it is the calculated effort to get into someone's good books.

The most important word in understanding this definition is deliberately. This is not about accidentally charming someone, or naturally getting along with people. Ingratiation is a conscious, planned behavior. You are choosing to act a certain way in order to produce a certain effect in someone else's mind — namely, that they like you, trust you, or feel warmly toward you.
The hidden motive — the soul of the word

What truly defines ingratiation and separates it from ordinary friendliness is the presence of a hidden goal. The person practicing ingratiation wants something. It could be a promotion, a favor, protection from someone's anger, social acceptance, financial gain, or simply more influence over a person. The pleasant behavior is a means to an end, not an honest expression of feeling.

This is why ingratiation carries a slightly negative, suspicious flavor. It implies a gap between what a person is showing on the outside and what they are actually feeling or thinking on the inside. The smiles, the compliments, the helpfulness — they are performances, not sincerity.
How it is different from genuine kindness

This distinction is important and worth spending time on.

If you genuinely admire your colleague and tell them "You handled that so well," that is sincere praise. If you tell your colleague the same thing primarily because you want them to support your project next week, that is ingratiation. The words look identical from the outside. The difference lives entirely in your interior motive.

This is also why ingratiation can be difficult to detect. A skilled ingratiator behaves in ways that look completely natural and kind. The bad faith is invisible.

Ingratiation does not look the same in every situation. People use different methods depending on what they want and who they are trying to win over.

The most common method is flattery — offering compliments that are exaggerated, strategic, or not fully believed by the person giving them. "You're the most talented person in this company" said to a boss whose approval you're chasing is a classic example.

Another method is deliberate agreement — pretending to share someone's opinions, tastes, or values so they feel a sense of connection with you. If your manager loves a particular sports team and you suddenly become a passionate fan of that team, that is ingratiation through manufactured common ground.

People also use favor-doing — going out of their way to help someone, not because they genuinely care, but to create a sense of warmth or obligation in the other person. And sometimes people use self-presentation tactics, carefully shaping how they appear — through behavior, appearance, or storytelling — to match what they think the other person finds appealing.

In reality, ingratiators often combine several of these at once, which is part of what makes the behavior feel so slippery and hard to pin down.
The verb you will always see alongside this noun

You will rarely encounter "ingratiation" without also seeing the verb "to ingratiate oneself" (with someone). This phrase means to make yourself liked or accepted by someone through deliberate, often calculated behavior. For example: "She ingratiates herself with powerful people wherever she goes." Understanding this verb will make the noun feel even more natural to you.
The connotation: slightly negative, but not always evil

Ingratiation is not a neutral word. It leans negative because it implies a kind of social manipulation — using charm or helpfulness as a tool rather than expressing it genuinely. When you call someone's behavior "ingratiation," you are suggesting they are not being fully honest, that there is an agenda behind their pleasantness.

That said, ingratiation is not always malicious or deeply harmful. It exists on a wide spectrum. On the mild end, it is something nearly everyone does in some form — dressing a little more impressively for a job interview, or being extra agreeable when meeting a partner's parents for the first time. These are soft, low-stakes versions of ingratiation and most people would consider them unremarkable.

On the more serious end, ingratiation can be a systematic and cynical strategy — a person who spends years carefully flattering a wealthy relative, pretending to share their values, and doing favors for them, all while planning to benefit from their will. This end of the spectrum is where ingratiation shades into manipulation and moral wrongdoing.
Where you will encounter this word

Ingratiation is most commonly discussed in the context of workplaces and careers — employees trying to win over managers, junior staff trying to impress senior executives, or salespeople trying to build false rapport with clients.

It also appears frequently in social and political settings — politicians performing warmth for voters, courtiers flattering royalty in historical accounts, or students trying to win favor with teachers.

You will also find it in psychology, where researchers have studied ingratiation as a social behavior pattern in depth. Psychologist Edward Jones, who studied this phenomenon closely, described it as a social influence strategy people use to make themselves appear attractive to others for personal benefit.
Example sentences to cement the meaning

• His constant ingratiation with the senior partners — praising every decision, laughing at every joke — was transparent to everyone except the partners themselves.
  • She was brilliant at ingratiation, knowing exactly what each person wanted to hear.
  • The new employee's ingratiation felt hollow; everyone could sense the ambition behind the smiles.
  • There is a fine line between networking and ingratiation — one is honest relationship-building, the other is a performance.

Ingratiation is the deliberate act of making yourself liked or favored by someone through calculated behavior — flattery, agreement, favors, or careful self-presentation — typically because you want something from them or want to advance your own interests. It implies a gap between what is shown and what is truly felt, which is why the word carries a mildly suspicious, critical tone. It is not always deeply wrong, but it is never quite fully honest. The moment kindness becomes a strategy rather than a feeling, it has crossed into ingratiation.
